# An Introduction to the Toy Supply Chain Category


By[Sarah Mouton Dowdy](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/sarah-mouton-dowdy) , *Content Marketing Manager*


Last Updated October 30, 2026


7 min read


Contrary to popular belief, the toy supply chain category isn’t all fun and games, at least not from the perspective of suppliers that must navigate its complicated demand patterns.


The toy category typically conjures images of retail shelves brimming with board games, babydolls, action figures, and the like. These are often described as **evergreen lines** , or toys that are sold throughout the year and peak at certain times.


But visit your local retailers in the days leading up to holidays like Halloween and Christmas, and you’re likely to see a different subcategory of toys: seasonal, holiday-themed knickknacks like ghost stuffies and Grinch puzzles. These items have a retail window of around 6–10 weeks and lose most of their value once the holiday passes.


Suppliers of both kinds of toys must navigate two very different supply chain realities, while also following specific safety rules and regulations.


**This article provides a general overview of the toy supply chain category for new or prospective toy suppliers. Read it to learn:**


-


What the toy category includes and excludes


-


Why evergreen toy lines and holiday goods follow different planning calendars


-


Safety testing and electronic Certificate of Compliance filing requirements


-


Where suppliers can find more guidance on[retailer compliance and deductions](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/)


## What Is Included in the Toys Supply Chain Category?


The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) defines a toy as[any object designed, manufactured, or marketed as a plaything for children under 14](https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Business-Education/Toy-Safety) . Citing Circana Checkout data, The Toy Association splits U.S. toys into 11 categories and highlights that[U.S. retail toy sales reached $30.3 billion in 2025](https://www.toyassociation.org/ta/toys/research-and-data/data/us-sales-data.aspx) . Games and puzzles led at $4.9 billion, followed by building sets at $4.3 billion, and outdoor and sports toys at $4.0 billion.

Toys within these super categories can be further categorized into evergreen and seasonal/holiday toys.


-


**Evergreen toys** line retailer shelves (both physical and digital) year-round and experience seasonal peaks.


-


**Seasonal/holiday toys** are produced and purchased for a particular calendar moment, such as a Valentine-themed doll or Easter bunny bouncy ball.


### What Does the Toy Category Exclude?


According to the CPSC definition, the following items are not included in the toy category:


-


Bicycles and tricycles


-


Non-powered scooters as defined in ASTM F2264


-


Recreational powered scooters and pocket bikes as defined in ASTM F2641


-


Sling shots and sharp-pointed darts


-


Playground equipment


-


Non-powder guns


-


Kites


-


Hobby and craft items in which the finished item is not primarily of play value


-


Model kits in which the finished item is not primarily of play value


-


Crayons, paints, chalks, and other similar art materials in which the material itself or the finished item is not primarily of play value


-


Sporting goods, camping goods, athletic equipment, musical instruments, juvenile products, and furniture (except the toy counterparts of such products)


-


Powered models of aircraft, rockets, boats, and land vehicles (except the toy counterparts of such products)


-


Constant air inflatables (i.e., an inflatable that relies on an electric blower at all times, such as a bounce house)


## Why Do Evergreen and Seasonal Toys Run on Two Different Clocks?


Evergreen toys sell at a relatively predictable rate all year, with a lift in Q4. Holiday-specific items, on the other hand, have a demand window that lasts mere weeks. For example, a Valentine’s plush has almost no value on February 15th. This asymmetry in demand drives differences in planning, production, inventory, shelf logic, and shipping.


#### *Planning and Production Calendars*


Seasonal items are planned backward from a fixed “in-store by” date. Design and buyer commitments often happen 9–12 months or more in advance, factory production runs months before the season, and then you need to leave room for logistics.


Evergreen items run on a rolling cycle: forecast, replenish, reorder. Factories can produce these goods in continuous or repeating runs, and inventory is managed with ongoing replenishment rather than one big bet.


#### *Inventory Risk*


With evergreen, a forecast miss is a manageable problem. Unsold stock keeps its value and can sit on the shelf. With seasonal, a miss is costly. Leftover stock gets marked down, stored for a year (with carrying costs and possible packaging wear), or liquidated.


Because there’s typically one shot at the buy, seasonal orders tend to be more conservative on quantity, with fewer opportunities for in-season reorders since factory lead times often exceed the season itself.


#### *Retail Shelf Logic*


Seasonal products get temporary placement, with a defined set date, a peak, and a markdown or clearance phase. Evergreen products hold permanent planogram space. That means seasonal suppliers are working to retailer-set calendars, which tend to be earlier than consumers expect (Halloween and Christmas products appearing in late summer, for instance).


#### *Shipping and Logistics*


Seasonal goods compete for container space and port capacity at peak times, and a delay of even a couple of weeks can be disastrous. Evergreen shipments have more flexibility, so they can be consolidated, rerouted, or expedited without the product’s value collapsing.

## What Does Toy Compliance Require Before a Shipment Moves?


Toy suppliers must adhere to CPSC safety and filing requirements.


### Safety Rules and Certification for Toys


The Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act (CPSIA) made[ASTM F963 a mandatory safety standard for children’s toys](https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Business-Education/Toy-Safety) . Toys manufactured after April 20, 2024, must meet ASTM F963-23. The standard covers areas such as small parts, sound levels, batteries, magnets, and lead content, though not every section applies to every toy.


Manufacturers and importers of children’s products must also issue a[Children’s Product Certificate](https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Testing-Certification/Childrens-Product-Certificate) , which rests on testing at a CPSC-accepted third-party lab. Children’s toys also need[tracking labels](https://www.cpsc.gov/Business--Manufacturing/Business-Education/tracking-label) on the product and its packaging, along with the producer’s name and address and required labels such as age grading.


### CPSC Certificate of Compliance Filing for Toys at Customs Entry


The CPSC has required a Certificate of Compliance to be on file to import covered products since 2008. But as of July 8, 2026, importers must file Certificate of Compliance data electronically with the Customs Entry for regulated consumer products. Missing or inaccurate data can delay entry or hold cargo.


There are two ways to submit this necessary data.[According to UPS](https://www.ups.com/gb/en/shipping/international-shipping/tariffs/cpsc) , importers may “submit a full message set of the seven data elements from the Certificate of Compliance through a PGA message set for each product in each shipment,” or simply upload their product’s certificate data into the[CPSC product registry website](https://www.cpsc.gov/eFiling-CPSC-Product-Registry) .


UPS notes that this update doesn't change which products and articles are subject to CPSC standards and regulations and clarifies that the electronic filing requirement applies to all products subject to CPSC regulations, regardless of shipment value.


**Related Reading:**[How to Generate a Best-In-Class Compliance Program](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/how-to-generate-a-best-in-class-compliance-program)


## Why Do Toy Retailer Deductions Cost More for Holiday Toys?


Retailers measure ship windows and penalize misses in both directions. Target’s compliance policy (as updated in 2024)[charges 5% of cost of goods on units delivered early or late](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/target-compliance-policy-update) against the shipping window. On an evergreen toy line, this charge is the main cost of a miss, as the product can still sell later. But for holiday toys, goods that reach the shelf after the shopping period lose more than compliance deductions, and holiday windows leave less room to recover from a miss.
